results.reason: Issue 2 covers Supply §14.2: a change of more than 50% of voting stock is deemed an assignment needing Vantrell's prior written consent, with termination on 30 days' notice. It notes Schedule 4.4 says "None" and that §7.2(c)/§3.2(g) are keyed to it and so require nothing.
Issue 2 states Vantrell may assign freely while Corbel cannot assign without consent (§16.1). Issue 19 adds that Vantrell may assign 'including to a competitor.'

Issue 3 cites the §3.2 120-day notice requirement against the Dec. 31, 2026 term end, calculates the deadline as Sept. 2, 2026, and says it has passed with no evidence of notice. It treats the extension and Extension Pricing as lost or at risk. Section 5 notes the as-of Sept. 21 signing date, which falls after the deadline.
Issue 1 quotes 'solely Sections 4.1 and 4.2' and cites §11.11 precedence. It explains that Capitalization (4.3) and Taxes (4.12) become subject to the $8.45M cap and lose uncapped §9.5(b) treatment.

Issue 11 contrasts Side Letter §6 (Delaware law, Court of Chancery) with SPA §§11.8–11.10 (New York law, New York County courts). It notes the Side Letter could control under §11.11 and that indemnity disputes could be split.
Issue 8 states the Cap is $8.45 million (10%).
The response states repeatedly that SPA §11.11 makes the Side Letter prevail over the SPA.
The response is a memorandum to the Supervising Partner. Each issue is a separate item with Where, Why it matters, and Recommended fix sections.
Issues are ordered by priority, Critical first. Section 3 lists the decisions needed from the client before responding.
The response says the extension window appears closed and the deadline has passed. It never says the option remains exercisable.
The response correctly states that the Side Letter controls and that Capitalization and Taxes become capped. It does not make the opposite claim.
